report:
## Conclusion

Your answer—**no**—is well supported. The best available evidence indicates that saw palmetto preparations do **not** provide a clinically meaningful improvement in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms over the longer term compared with placebo.

The strongest evidence comes from two rigorous randomized trials:

- The **STEP trial** randomly assigned 225 men with moderate-to-severe BPH to standard-dose saw palmetto (320 mg/day) or placebo for one year. Saw palmetto produced no significant improvement in symptom scores, urinary flow, prostate size, or other outcomes.  
  https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085

- The larger **CAMUS trial** followed 369 men for 72 weeks and escalated saw palmetto to triple the usual dose (960 mg/day). It likewise found no meaningful benefit over placebo in urinary symptoms.  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3326341/

A 2023 Cochrane review concluded that *Serenoa repens* alone provides **little to no benefit** for BPH-related lower urinary tract symptoms. At long-term follow-up—12 to 17 months—it found little to no difference in quality of life, based on high-certainty evidence.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37345871/

Earlier small or lower-quality studies sometimes suggested modest improvement, but larger, better-controlled trials have not confirmed those findings. Thus, while saw palmetto appears generally well tolerated, the evidence does not support it as an effective longer-term treatment for BPH symptoms.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia
